# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## DEVONthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. ## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

# Drafts Inbox

Triage the items sitting in the Drafts **inbox** — your capture-to-action pipeline. Archiving each item when it's handled means the inbox itself is the "unprocessed since last run" queue; there's no separate timestamp to track.

## When to Use

Use this skill at the start of a session or whenever you want to process items you've captured throughout the day via Drafts on iPhone, Apple Watch, or Mac.

## Prerequisites

- Drafts MCP connector must be set up.

## Instructions

1. Read the inbox with `drafts_get_drafts` (`folder: "inbox"`). This returns summaries only (title, dates, flags, tags), not full content.
2. **Check the volume first.** If the inbox is large (more than ~20 items, i.e. a backlog rather than a session's worth), don't try to process everything blindly. Report the count and date range, and ask how far back to go (e.g. this month, last 3 months, flagged only, or the whole backlog). Default to the most recent window.
   - The MCP returns the full inbox; use the `modificationDate` field to filter to the chosen window yourself. `drafts_get_drafts` also accepts `modifiedAfter` / `flagged` to narrow the pull.
3. Present a numbered list of the in-scope items with a brief preview of each.
4. For each item, pull its full content with `drafts_get_draft` (the summary title is truncated), classify it, and take the appropriate action:

| Type | Action |
|------|--------|
| **Task or to-do** | Capture to OmniFocus via `omnifocus-capture` (inbox by default). Flag if urgent. |
| **Writing idea (substantial)** | Create a Writing Task in `APR/TaskNotes/Tasks/` (frontmatter: `status`, `priority`, `dateCreated`/`dateModified`, `tags: [task]`, `ContentType: Blog`/`Newsletter`/`Glossary`). |
| **Content hook (one-liner)** | Add to the running `APR/Efforts/Content Ideas.md` note. |
| **Research request** | Do the research and report findings. |
| **Quick instruction** | Execute the instruction (file a note, move a file, look something up). |
| **Question** | Answer the question. |
| **Reference / clipping** | File it where it belongs (vault note, DevonThink, etc.) or note that it's already captured elsewhere. |
| **Unclear** | Ask for clarification before acting. |

5. After processing each item, archive the draft with `drafts_archive`.
6. Report what was done: "[N] items processed. [Brief summary of actions taken.]"

## Rules

- Process items one at a time. Don't batch everything silently. (For a large backlog, a grouped proposal with a per-item action is fine, but get approval before archiving or capturing anything.)
- When an item is ambiguous, ask rather than guess.
- Archive each draft only after it's been fully processed — the archive is what marks it "done," so never archive something you skipped.
- If an item requires a tool you don't have access to, note it and move on (leave it in the inbox).
- Confirm before deleting; default to archive, not trash.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error.   "id": "860BEADB-FDFF-4E57-9F41-796D9864A4D1",
  "title": "Reshuffle",
  "content": "Reshuffle

The music industry is a good example of the change that is being unleashed by AI.

Music came in albums and required a record company's backing because of the pressing costs for the vinyl and the need for distribution network.

Digital music reduces those costs and so albums become less important and singles more important.

Spotify, Apple Music et al, become arise because they become the way people find music.

In the process much of the old music industry died.
--
Using Shein, with all of it's flaws, as another example - the work heirarchy has been completely inverted. There aren't long meetings about reducing risk. There aren't seasonal cycles, they run small experiments, if an item takes off they do more, if it fails they look for another.experiment.

There are no silos and limited coordination overhead.

Ignoring the ethical and environmental implications of the way they do business, they're a very agile organization.

Shein's success isn't about doing individual tasks faster, but deliver the outcomes that the audience wants sooner.
--
## Ch 5 Rebundling the Job
Core claim - in a world where everyone has access to the same knowledge, there is knowledge overwhelm.

The promise of good taste and curation beats the promise of volume.

Leans into Theory of Constraints with a twist. Constraints are Scarcity, Risk and Coordination.

**Scarcity** - something that is a key resource is limited. In the case of shipping he shows that communications with the outside world - to keep up to date on schedule or summon help in emergency. So the radio operator with Morse code was the constraint. In modern software development the constraint is often Quality Assurance or Code Review.

**Risks** - Anaesthesiologist in a surgical environment. They're managing risk in the surgery. Paying attention to the patient's vital signs. Too much anaesthetic and the patients organs will shut down. Too little and they will wake up in the midst of the surgery.

**Coordination** - Many moving parts that need to align across groups. The book's example is getting a movie made. From writing, actors, sets, costumes, cinematography, funding, editing and ... . In this world the Producer is the coordinator and the becomes the constraint.

When all wine, good, bad and awful became more widely available the value of the sommelier increased. Wine is no longer scarce. Further, the internet is full of reviews about wine and vineyards. The constraint now is knowing where to look and who to trust. The sommelier is curating and instilling confidence. A restaurant uses them now as part of a package, promising people a better dining experience.

### Don't Chase the Skill, Follow the Constraint
Up skilling is still valuable, but only in the context of understanding the constraints first. Look to where the scarcity, risk or coordination constraints are and up skill for those problems.

> Skills are only valuable in relation to solving a constraint.

The evolution of the role of radiologists is a good example. They go from interpreting scans, to providing context for their colleagues. A shadow on a lung has a different meaning depending on the history of a patient. They participate more in the discussion of how to treat a cancer. *The implied claim that AI would get better than humans at reading X-ray and other images, still hasn't panned out.*

When constraints change, the roles that had value in the old case lose value. However, new roles emerge to tackle the new constraints.

The core claim of the book thus far: AI unbundles some tasks. Work that used to be valuable is no longer valuable. Instead of scarcity of skills, the constraints will be handling risk and coordination.

**Risks** with a new technology, we look for risks within the technology itself. Example elevators, the first question is what happens if the technology fails, will the elevator fall? The bigger risks come from the downstream effects. Elevators enable tall buildings, which have new structural and fire risks.

With GenAI one of the added layers of risk is the probabilistic nature of the systems.

**Coordination** tells a story of nurse navigators, helping patients deal with the increasingly messy journey through the hospital system. They use their expertise to coordinate. In the process they reduce the stress level for the patient and shorten the hospital stay.

The AI tools made some areas/departments work faster, but they were silos. The author calls this narrow. The nurse coordinator is working broadly across the whole system.

*We get to this better place, by helping people see the whole system and not the parts.*

==We only get rewarded when the value is made visible. It's not enough to improve the system if people don't see the value created.==

*Tidbit* - As AI execution scales, handling the exceptions (i.e. mislabel bins, damaged parts) becomes a much larger and more important job. The people who do this work in a warehouse do it informally and so are rarely noticed. It shows up in care environments, the system pays people for the task, yet the biggest value is the emotional support they provide.

Part of reimagining work will require making the invisible work (value?), visible to the system.

## Ch 6 Rebundling the Organization
Real Madrid, mid 2000s, built around star players. All given autonomy, yet they produced mediocre results. They optimized for individual play and didn't have a system. Barcelona, succeeded by having a system and giving players freedom within their zone.

The more complex the system, the more specialized the parts, the more important for there to be an explicit coordination system. Real Madrid failed because they lacked a system.

Mars Climate Orbiter is another example of coordination failure. One team did their math in pound-force and the other Newtons. Each team trusted the others competence and didn't question the numbers, they were experts after all. Small errors accumulated. The navigation system believed it was in the right place. When it tried to enter orbit, it instead hit the thin atmosphere and burned up. The teams had worked in isolation.

### Reducing the Coordination Tax with AI
The author claims that AI eliminates the tax. I'm troubled because he's ignoring the possibility of hallucination and the biases that the AI will add in.

He cites NotebookLLM, good. But also Persona generation. Not so good.

Leaning very heavily into Agentic execution to scout out and book sales calls -> agents to select suppliers.

Another good example is that burden of expense reporting has gone away. An AI pulls receipts from inboxes, categorizes and then sends them to the right people for approval. *Neither the employee, nor finance are dealing with the mess of expenses. A coordination tax has been eliminated*

  "title": "If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI related topics, this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).",
  "content": "If your current feelings on GenAI are, it's a steaming mess and should be buried you might be right. You also might want to skip this newsletter. I'm going to touch on a few AI related topics, this week, starting with the Canadian government’s AI strategy (or lack thereof).

## Canadian Government AI Strategy
Unlike many news outlets, I can’t do instant analysis and reflective thinking. I need to time to noodle and digest. There is some good in the strategy: emphasis on safety and education. Sovereignty sounds like a good idea, until you realize that it just means build more data centres and invest in Canadian AI companies.

The real problem is that the strategy, defines the key pillar "Powering AI adoption for shared prosperity". When you dig into that pillar, we discover that they're measuring AI adoption as a proxy for prosperity/productivity. This is very funny, I'm sure we've all seen plenty of examples of AI adoption, where someone takes bullet points and asks ChatGPT to create a presentation. Faster than doing it manually? Yes. Did anyone want that presentation? Did the person created it learn anything meaningful about the topic? Making the wrong thing go faster is not productivity.

The strategy selects five areas to focus AI productivity on: Healthcare, Agriculture, Manufacturing, Energy and Natural Resources, and Transportation. I  know a bit about healthcare and so I focused on that [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/).

Instead of dealing with the hard work of making systemic improvements to the healthcare (or other) system, the strategy is betting on a magic wand.

I'm also thinking that we will see a lot of "AI Washing" in the next few years. Changes that were already in progress will be rebranded as AI. I think existing machine learning, will be rebranded as AI.

## From AI Washing to Bigger isn’t always Better
In booster circles, I hear two suggestions: Just use agents and don’t worry next weeks model will solve all the existing problems.

I've had two experiences in the past few weeks that highlight the problem with both suggestions. I used Claude Fable to do a security audit of the Personal Expense Tracker App, I’m building. I accidentally used agents to with Claude Opus, when I wanted to understand what lead magnets currently work to get people to sign up for a newsletter.

### Fable Security Audit
Anthropic has limited access to the Fable model, which they previously touted for its ability to do security audits. Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to Fable to do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s work experience with Fable, its success is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect, it used all my Claude subscription for a 5hr period and required another block later that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi 3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8. The Kimi 3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better by massive amounts of RAM and compute. So progress, by throwing more of everything at the problem.

### Opus Research Task
I asked Opus to do some research, on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further it decided that it would use 3 voting rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my 5hr block and needed block later that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with a real depth. Instead, I got a 3 page report, with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

## Big Ask
One of the two insights from Opus's Research Task? Ask your newsletter readers for referrals to quote Opus: "single most effective newsletter growth strategy is **direct recommendations from existing subscribers (word-of-mouth/referral)**". I'm supposed to offer you and your a discount or a free trial in return. In practice, I can't see what I would offer at the moment.

If you get value from this newsletter, please share it with a friend. If someone shared it with you, click here to subscribe.

Since I'm building an application and I'm not a security expert, I thought it would be helpful to Fable to do an audit. Based on reviewing other people’s work experience with Fable, its success is chaining together multiple steps into a single exploit. Sure enough, it found one key vulnerability and a bunch of minor ones. What I didn’t expect, it used all my Claude subscription for a 5hr period and required another block later that evening. The best part? My security flaw was the result of a hastily implemented bug fix from earlier in the week. 

The frontier labs don't generally talk about how how their models are getting better. However, looking at the open weight models, we can make some good guesses. Kimi 3 was just released and it claims to be in the same league as Claude Opus 4.8. The Kimi 3 model is 2.8 Trillion parameters. Assuming we can compare it to Opus and Fable, these models are getting better by massive amounts of RAM and compute. So progress, by throwing more of everything at the problem.

I asked Opus to do some research, on lead magnets. I mistakenly asked for "deep research" - don't do this unless you want to spend a lot of tokens in a few minutes. Opus decided to spin up agents to do the work. The idea was that each agent would a small task and then report back. The central agent would combine the results and report back. Further it decided that it would use 3 voting rule. For each idea three agents were asked to analyse a different source. Then the individual agents were asked to vote on the claim they were analysing. The result was that 50 claims were evaluated by 150 agents. It took 30 minutes to burn through my 5hr block and needed block later that evening to finish the task.

For that much compute, I was expecting a nice long report with a real depth. Instead, I got a 3 page report, with two good insights.

Agents are not necessarily better. I may well need a much longer blog post to explain why. The short version: assume each agent is imperfect at the task. You can't mask the imperfections of one agent with another. If anything, I would expect the imperfections to multiply.

  "content": "BDD notes

- One paper was around testing UI PostHoc - well done and not useful.
See Panda Post
- Has anyone written a good BDD discovery coach. Could I turn the example mapping blog post into a discovery tool?
- Automating creation of Playwright tests and also **interpreting results**
- BDD collaboration - most important in cases of: complexity; Regulatory; Legacy

Current generation reasoning relies on statistical pattern matching. Reasoning responses are often just replicating patterns seen in training data. This is not a logical deduction.

Code and architectural quality in general, Models suffer in their attempts to create good quality code:
- trained on a mass of code across the internet -> No coherent principles involved
- training data isn't grounded in OO, Functional Programming or any other principles -> can be added by use "skills" et al however this is a context consuming band-aid
- May follow unconventional patterns making it harder to understand
- Doesn't know the problem domain it's being asked to work in.
- Doesn't have access to all of the relevant data. Code, User Stories, etc and not all stored in the same place. In addition they're often not written in the same language 
- Context windows are still a problem - even models with large context windows often 'forget' to pay attention to the bits in the middle

10 yrs ago, we all knew not to blindly paste StackOverflow code into our products. Now we do that every day and call it productivity.

  "content": "Economic disruption could affect growth for years, Macklem warnsMARK RENDELL ECONOMICS REPORTER

The Globe and Mail (Ottawa/Quebec Edition)
Feb 06, 2026

BoC chief says lower interest rates can’t cushion the country’s structural transformation

The Canadian economy is going through a profound structural transformation that could weigh on growth for years, but further interest rate cuts risk doing more harm than good, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Thursday.

A combination of U. S. protectionism, artificial intelligence and a sharp slowdown in population growth is fundamentally changing the Canadian economy, Mr. Macklem said in a speech to a Bay Street audience in Toronto.

Canadian companies have begun to adjust to this new world. But this process will take “years, not quarters,” he said, with major risks if the economy fails to restructure.

“The transition could be faster than we expect, particularly if trade uncertainties ease and businesses move more boldly to invest in new technology, markets and products. But it could also be more painful than we’d like – particularly if the trade situation darkens or other shocks disrupt the economy,” he said.

The governor urged business leaders and politicians to “lean into” these forces by developing new international markets and adopting artificial intelligence tools to boost productivity.

But he was circumspect about the role the Bank of Canada can play during this period of disruption, offering a somewhat hawkish take on monetary policy that reinforced market expectations that the central bank will remain on hold through 2026.

Last week, the bank held its benchmark interest rate steady at 2.25 per cent for the second consecutive time. And it signalled that further cuts are unlikely unless there is a significant change to the economic outlook.

“We have to be careful not to misdiagnose economic weakness. Monetary policy should not try to compensate for lost supply,” Mr. Macklem said Thursday, expanding on the bank’s current thinking about interest rates, economic growth and inflation.

If the economy was going through a regular cyclical downturn, then it might make sense to stimulate demand by easing interest rates, he said. But if economic weakness is being caused by structural forces – such as a reordering of North American supply chains or sudden drop in immigration levels – then the argument shifts.

“Lowering interest rates in the face of weak economic activity risks stoking future inflation if the weakness is due to lower productive capacity rather than a cyclical downturn in demand. And there is also a risk that overstimulating demand when the problem is structural could delay needed structural change,” he said.

Annual Consumer Price Index growth has been inside the bank’s 1per- cent to 3- per- cent control band for a year, and the bank is forecasting that it will remain around 2- per- cent over the next year. Still, Mr. Macklem’s comment suggests he remains wary of upside risks to inflation, even as the economy struggles to churn out much growth.

Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said that Mr. Macklem’s speech stood in stark contrast to the views of Kevin Warsh, U. S. President Donald Trump’s pick to be the next chair of the U. S. Federal Reserve. Mr.

Warsh has argued that strong productivity growth from the adoption of artificial intelligence should allow the Fed to ease rates without stoking inflation.

“The freshly- nominated

Fed Chair believes that monetary policy can help accelerate the structural transition underway, with lower interest rates supporting business spending on productivity- enhancing investments. Only time will tell which central banker is correct,” Mr. Mendes wrote in a note to clients.

“However, with inflationary pressures already very tame in Canada, Macklem sounded unnecessarily hawkish on the outlook for rates,” Mr. Mendes added.

The Canadian economy has proven more resilient over the past year than many economists expected, but it remains in a funk. Exports are down sharply, unemployment is elevated and businesses are postponing investment and hiring decisions.

Canada’s real gross domestic product flatlined in November and appears to have contracted slightly in the fourth quarter, according to GDP numbers published by Statistics Canada last week.

Looking ahead, the Bank of Canada forecast muted GDP growth of 1.1 per cent in 2026 and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

“In our baseline forecast, the spillover effects from the trade shock and uncertainty gradually dissipate and the economy recovers from the cyclical weakness. But the path for potential output is lower because of increased trade friction and slower population growth,” Mr. Macklem said.

A great deal depends on U. S. trade policy, particularly the outcome of the upcoming review of the North American free- trade pact, known as USMCA.

Most Canadian exports remain exempt from U. S. tariffs, owing to a carveout for products that comply with trade- agreement rules. If that exemption were to end, the effective tariff rate would rise sharply, with grave consequences for the Canadian economy.

Mr. Macklem said that Canadian companies, supported by government fiscal and industrial policy, have begun to make the adjustments necessary to thrive in a rapidly changing world. But it’s still early going.

Canadian exports to countries other than the U. S. have risen over the past year. But this has been driven by certain idiosyncratic factors, such as the surge in the price of gold, and so far companies are mostly shipping more products to existing clients rather than developing new overseas markets.

The story is similar for the adoption of artificial intelligence, which “looks to be increasing in Canada but remains modest,” Mr. Macklem said.

Only 8 per cent of businesses surveyed by the Bank of Canada reported significant AI use in their operations, while another 11 per cent reported plans to use AI over the next year, he said.

Going forward, Canada’s ability to diversify trade and adopt new technologies will determine the country’s future prosperity, he said.

“We can be victims of U. S. tariffs and AI disruption, or we can lean into structural change, expand our internal market, diversify our trade, embrace new technology and raise our productivity.”

  "content": "Economic disruption could affect growth for years, Macklem warnsMARK RENDELL ECONOMICS REPORTER

The Globe and Mail (Ottawa/Quebec Edition)
Feb 06, 2026

BoC chief says lower interest rates can’t cushion the country’s structural transformation

The Canadian economy is going through a profound structural transformation that could weigh on growth for years, but further interest rate cuts risk doing more harm than good, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Thursday.

A combination of U. S. protectionism, artificial intelligence and a sharp slowdown in population growth is fundamentally changing the Canadian economy, Mr. Macklem said in a speech to a Bay Street audience in Toronto.

Canadian companies have begun to adjust to this new world. But this process will take “years, not quarters,” he said, with major risks if the economy fails to restructure.

“The transition could be faster than we expect, particularly if trade uncertainties ease and businesses move more boldly to invest in new technology, markets and products. But it could also be more painful than we’d like – particularly if the trade situation darkens or other shocks disrupt the economy,” he said.

The governor urged business leaders and politicians to “lean into” these forces by developing new international markets and adopting artificial intelligence tools to boost productivity.

But he was circumspect about the role the Bank of Canada can play during this period of disruption, offering a somewhat hawkish take on monetary policy that reinforced market expectations that the central bank will remain on hold through 2026.

Last week, the bank held its benchmark interest rate steady at 2.25 per cent for the second consecutive time. And it signalled that further cuts are unlikely unless there is a significant change to the economic outlook.

“We have to be careful not to misdiagnose economic weakness. Monetary policy should not try to compensate for lost supply,” Mr. Macklem said Thursday, expanding on the bank’s current thinking about interest rates, economic growth and inflation.

If the economy was going through a regular cyclical downturn, then it might make sense to stimulate demand by easing interest rates, he said. But if economic weakness is being caused by structural forces – such as a reordering of North American supply chains or sudden drop in immigration levels – then the argument shifts.

“Lowering interest rates in the face of weak economic activity risks stoking future inflation if the weakness is due to lower productive capacity rather than a cyclical downturn in demand. And there is also a risk that overstimulating demand when the problem is structural could delay needed structural change,” he said.

Annual Consumer Price Index growth has been inside the bank’s 1per- cent to 3- per- cent control band for a year, and the bank is forecasting that it will remain around 2- per- cent over the next year. Still, Mr. Macklem’s comment suggests he remains wary of upside risks to inflation, even as the economy struggles to churn out much growth.

Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said that Mr. Macklem’s speech stood in stark contrast to the views of Kevin Warsh, U. S. President Donald Trump’s pick to be the next chair of the U. S. Federal Reserve. Mr.

Warsh has argued that strong productivity growth from the adoption of artificial intelligence should allow the Fed to ease rates without stoking inflation.

“The freshly- nominated

Fed Chair believes that monetary policy can help accelerate the structural transition underway, with lower interest rates supporting business spending on productivity- enhancing investments. Only time will tell which central banker is correct,” Mr. Mendes wrote in a note to clients.

“However, with inflationary pressures already very tame in Canada, Macklem sounded unnecessarily hawkish on the outlook for rates,” Mr. Mendes added.

The Canadian economy has proven more resilient over the past year than many economists expected, but it remains in a funk. Exports are down sharply, unemployment is elevated and businesses are postponing investment and hiring decisions.

Canada’s real gross domestic product flatlined in November and appears to have contracted slightly in the fourth quarter, according to GDP numbers published by Statistics Canada last week.

Looking ahead, the Bank of Canada forecast muted GDP growth of 1.1 per cent in 2026 and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

“In our baseline forecast, the spillover effects from the trade shock and uncertainty gradually dissipate and the economy recovers from the cyclical weakness. But the path for potential output is lower because of increased trade friction and slower population growth,” Mr. Macklem said.

A great deal depends on U. S. trade policy, particularly the outcome of the upcoming review of the North American free- trade pact, known as USMCA.

Most Canadian exports remain exempt from U. S. tariffs, owing to a carveout for products that comply with trade- agreement rules. If that exemption were to end, the effective tariff rate would rise sharply, with grave consequences for the Canadian economy.

Mr. Macklem said that Canadian companies, supported by government fiscal and industrial policy, have begun to make the adjustments necessary to thrive in a rapidly changing world. But it’s still early going.

Canadian exports to countries other than the U. S. have risen over the past year. But this has been driven by certain idiosyncratic factors, such as the surge in the price of gold, and so far companies are mostly shipping more products to existing clients rather than developing new overseas markets.

The story is similar for the adoption of artificial intelligence, which “looks to be increasing in Canada but remains modest,” Mr. Macklem said.

Only 8 per cent of businesses surveyed by the Bank of Canada reported significant AI use in their operations, while another 11 per cent reported plans to use AI over the next year, he said.

Going forward, Canada’s ability to diversify trade and adopt new technologies will determine the country’s future prosperity, he said.

“We can be victims of U. S. tariffs and AI disruption, or we can lean into structural change, expand our internal market, diversify our trade, embrace new technology and raise our productivity.”

  "title": "Agile practitioners are currently navigating a profound structural and philosophical transition, shifting from manual facilitators to "orchestrators" who use AI to manage administrative "grunt work" while simultaneously facing existential fears regarding job devaluation and the rise of "management-b…",
  "content": "Agile practitioners are currently navigating a profound structural and philosophical transition, shifting from manual facilitators to "orchestrators" who use AI to manage administrative "grunt work" while simultaneously facing existential fears regarding job devaluation and the rise of "management-by-dashboard".

### **Emotional Responses**

The emotional climate within the Agile community is a complex tapestry of conflicting sentiments triggered by rapid technological shifts:

- **Hope:** Practitioners feel a sense of relief at the prospect of **"cognitive decoupling"**, where AI handles administrative "grunt work" like ticket formatting and retrospective synthesis. They hope this allows a return to core human coaching, such as fostering high-performance team dynamics.
- **Fear:** This is primarily triggered by **"Reductions in Force" (RIFs)** and organizational restructuring where "Agile Coach" roles are targeted for elimination. There is anxiety about the **"Great Hiring Implosion,"** where machines are perceived to hire other machines, alienating humans from the talent lifecycle.
- **Anger:** Many are infuriated by **"Agile Theater Chaos,"** where AI is used to mask managerial incompetence or generate hollow, professional-sounding communications that lack genuine Agile commitment.
- **Excitement:** There is a sense of "weird fantasy" among those achieving **"10x" productivity gains**, using tools to build in minutes what previously took an entire sprint.
- **Resignation:** Some have accepted that AI adoption is **inevitable** and are focusing on survival and reskilling, believing AI will eventually "hack the operating system of human civilization".

### **Current Context**

The modern practitioner's environment has shifted from manual ceremony animation to high-level orchestration:

- **Current Tools:**
    - **Specialised Agents:** Tools like **Telos** and **Vomoai** are used to consolidate notes from Slack, emails, and calls to draft Jira tickets.
    - **Custom GPTs:** The **"Retrospective Insights Analyst"** GPT processes raw data from Miro boards to identify friction points human facilitators might miss.
    - **Transcription Engines:** Used to automate sprint transcriptions and summarize user research.
    - **Morale Tools:** Some use **Suno AI** to generate "Pep Songs" for teams during difficult sprint demos.
- **Typical Workday:** Practitioners spend their mornings on **"Morning Orchestration,"** reviewing AI summaries of asynchronous stand-ups and code commits to find blockers. This is followed by AI-assisted backlog refinement and strategic "entrepreneurial" tasks, such as testing business hypotheses.
- **Current Goals:** The primary goal is to **scale coaching** across 3--4 teams simultaneously by offloading "synthesis grunt work" to AI.

### **Specific Pain Points**

Practitioners have documented concrete failures where AI implementation met operational reality:

- **Copy-Paste Fatigue:** A major frustration is the disjointed hand-off between AI chat interfaces and systems of record like Jira, which one practitioner found so **"impractical"** that writing tickets manually remained faster.
- **Literalness and Lack of Intuition:** AI coding assistants are "terrible at reading minds"; if a requirement is vague, the AI "goes off the rails".
- **"Vanilla" Personas:** In user-centered design, AI-generated personas often lack **"illegible" social and political nuances**, resulting in over-sanitized, unrealistic representations that miss core user problems.
- **Adaptations:**
    - **"Waterfall 2.0":** To compensate for AI's literalness, teams are spending **three times more time** on upfront design and writing 5-page specifications that read like legal contracts.
    - **Micro-Waterfalls:** Some teams run "small waterfall" cycles where they write a spec, have AI build it in minutes, and immediately validate it, maintaining Agile's release cadence while adding Waterfall's rigor.
    - **"Vibe-Coding":** Using AI for exploratory, rapid brainstorming before switching to strict "Spec" mode for execution.

### **Ideal Scenarios**

Practitioners use "magic wand" thinking to envision a future where AI serves as a guardian of team health:

- **Burnout Sentinel:** A wish for AI that can identify organizational issues like **burnout** or stress signals in communication patterns before they manifest as failures.
- **Real-time Behavioral Feedback:** An "AI Coach" that provides immediate feedback during meetings, pointing out an **"uneven distribution of speech"** or suggesting more open-ended questions.
- **Ultra-efficient Units:** A bold vision for teams to shrink into high-performing units of just **"2 people plus an AI"**that build products at the speed of thought.
- **What they hope WON'T happen:**
    - AI becoming a **"Machiavellian prince"** used by leadership to enforce bureaucratic control or eliminate "human sense-making".
    - A total **loss of essential human skills** and a "mediocrity" caused by overreliance on technology that makes teams fragile.


Drawing on the provided sources, the following perspectives represent the diverse roles navigating the intersection of Agile and AI. These details are structured to support the creation of realistic personas for customer discovery.

### **1. The "Entrepreneurial" Strategist**

This perspective views AI as a "superpower" for those who move beyond administrative tasks to focus on high-stakes business hypotheses.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** CTO, Product Lead, or "Agile Alchemist".
- **Demographics:** Large-scale public sector (e.g. NHS England), government AI incubators, or high-growth tech startups. Often high-level experience (CTO-level).
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Aims to achieve **"10x" impact** with small, high-functioning teams (fewer than 7 people). Needs tools for **"Morning Orchestration"** to review asynchronous stand-ups and code commits.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Hates "meeting entropy" and the "busywork singularity" where AI generates summaries of summaries. Fears that "hybrid work" is becoming an obsolete concept replaced by "blended work" where human agency is redistributed.
- **Work Environment:** Fast-flowing information environments (Slack, Teams, GitHub) where the goal is to "dance with" rather than master a colossal system.
- **Real Story/Quote:** One CTO noted that while AI can give you "a million prototypes," the real bottleneck is getting feedback: *"Artefacts are not really what we're here for... we are demonstrably optimising about a mile from the bottleneck"*.
* * *

### **2. The Overwhelmed "Scribe" (Backlog Manager)**

This role is currently the most vulnerable to AI displacement as their primary value--documentation and coordination--is easily automated.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Product Owner (PO), Junior Project Manager, or "Backlog Clerk".
- **Demographics:** Mid-to-large corporations; often has a "light CS background" (e.g. VBA/SQL) but is not a primary developer.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to consolidate "scattered context" from Slack, emails, and customer calls into Jira tickets without manual copy-pasting.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** **"Copy-paste fatigue"**--finding that moving text between AI and Jira is so friction-heavy that manual writing is faster. Fears the **"Great Hiring Implosion"** where machines hire machines, making their facilitation skills redundant.
- **Work Environment:** A "feature factory" where the focus is on specification over value.
- **Real Story/Quote:** A PO frustrated by scattered data asked: *"I spend a stupid amount of time writing tickets... not because the writing is hard, but because the context is scattered everywhere... Is everyone still doing this manually?"*.
* * *

### **3. The "Structuralist" Purist**

This perspective rejects AI for administrative tasks, arguing that if a Scrum Master is busy updating tickets, the system design is broken.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Senior Agile Coach, Scrum Master, or "Friction Fixer".
- **Demographics:** 20+ years of experience; high-income countries (Finland, USA, UK); often technical veterans.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Aims for **"Cognitive Decoupling"**--using AI only if it handles "synthesis grunt work" to allow a return to human coaching.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Infuriated by **"Agile Theater"** and the "Agile Industrial Complex". Fears AI will become a "Machiavellian prince" used by leadership to enforce bureaucratic control.
- **Work Environment:** Values "face-to-face conversation" and physical index cards over digital boards.
- **Real Story/Quote:** A veteran coach stated: *"I don't recognize Agile any more... the focus has shifted from developers to executives, mostly because executives can pay those sweet, sweet consulting contracts"*.
* * *

### **4. The "Technical Veteran" Coach**

A practitioner who insists that Agile coaching is ineffective without deep technical domain knowledge.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** Release Train Engineer (RTE) or Scrum Master with a former Software Engineering background.
- **Demographics:** 35+ years in software; often age 60+; works in highly technical industries like Automotive or Telecomm.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to demonstrate **"Technical Competence"**--being able to walk the walk, like demonstrating a unit test or CI technique.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by Scrum Masters who measure themselves by "how many LEGO games they know" rather than understanding engineering blockers.
- **Work Environment:** Scaled Agile environments (SAFe) where they must eliminate dependencies to stay small.
- **Real Story/Quote:** One practitioner noted that AI coding assistants are mind-blind: *"If your requirements are vague, the AI goes off the rails... we are spending three times more time on upfront design and specifications"*.
* * *

### **5. The "Fuming" Executive**

A leadership perspective focused on ROI, often disillusioned with the speed of traditional Agile transformations.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** CEO, CFO, or "Operating Model Expert".
- **Demographics:** Large corporations or government agencies.
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs **"Management-by-Dashboard"** and clear metrics to justify the cost of Agile to stockholders.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by "conflicting priorities" among Agile leads that do not add up to strategic goals. Afraid that Agile is "not working for us" and seeks to "check the box" for transformation by the end of the year.
- **Work Environment:** The "Executive Board Room," often isolated from the "@GEMBA" (actual work floor).
- **Real Story/Quote:** A CEO in an Agile Theater scenario was described as *"fuming"* because *"None of the local priorities... add up to his own strategic priorities"*.
* * *

### **6. The User Research (UR) Specialist**

Focuses on capturing authentic user needs and is highly critical of AI's tendency to over-simplify human behavior.

- **Occupation/Role Specifics:** UX Researcher, Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Expert, or Persona Scientist.
- **Demographics:** Academic or specialized industry research roles; diverse international backgrounds (Finland, South Korea, Lebanon).
- **Stated Goals and Needs:** Needs to avoid **"Algorithmic Othering"** where minority identities are rendered hypervisible but inauthentic. Aims for "Human-Centered AI" (HCAI) protocols.
- **Frustrations and Fears:** Frustrated by **"Over-sanitization"**--AI omitting realistic negative traits or challenges to produce "unrealistically positive" user archetypes. Fears AI "hallucinations" where plausible-sounding user data has no basis in actual research.
- **Work Environment:** Laboratory or digital design settings focused on data-driven personas (DDPs).
- **Real Story/Quote:** A researcher found that in addiction studies, AI mixed up symptoms of different drugs: *"The personas consistently portrayed addiction narratives in an unrealistically positive light, minimizing the severity of substance abuse issues"*.

  "content": "I've posted many times about how GenAI is reducing critical thinking, as using it requires more critical thinking. That got me thinking, how can these tools help with Critical Thinking? For over 10yrs, I have encouraged potential ScrumMasters to use Systems Thinking to gain a deeper understanding of many of their challenges. I've tried to find analogies people can relate to, like a long line at the grocery store.

However, this is a big leap from going from the grocery store to applying the skill in our real work. Even the simplest approach to Systems Thinking asks the person doing the work to keep in mind several questions. That's where GenAI can play a role. I've created a Claude skill to help with the basics of Systems Thinking. Instead of trying to remember a list of questions, the user tells the AI the story of their problem, and the AI asks follow-up questions to uncover deeper issues.

The current version of the skill includes a core set of questions and a Causal Loop Diagramming skill. As I get feedback, I will expand the repository, possibly to include more mental models.

If you don't use Claude, Claude Skills are being more widely adopted as AgentSkills, and in the meantime, you can always copy the prompt into your own prompt library.

I built a Claude skill to save some effort: instead of memorizing a framework, you tell the AI your problem story. It asks the follow-up questions that uncover the deeper issues. Just tell your story and reflect on whether the GenAI is going in a useful direction.

The skill includes core Systems Thinking questions and Causal Loop Diagramming. As I get feedback, I'll expand it to include more mental models. If you don't use Claude, you can copy the prompt into your own AI tool.
